title: Odissi music: follow the singer
lead: A voice carries poetry into music. Follow the song, its teachers and its credits into Odisha’s vocal tradition.

paragraphs: Begin with a voice. At an Odissi performance, try following the singer through one complete phrase before returning your attention to the dancer. Which word holds your ear? Where does the voice linger? You do not need to name a raga to become curious about the person carrying the song.

Odissi music also has a life as a subject of vocal study. Utkal University of Culture’s syllabus approved in 2023 sets out a postgraduate programme in Odissi Vocal. It places theory, notation and practical singing beside one another. That document offers a useful doorway into a musical tradition that deserves attention beyond its role on a dance stage.

blocks.title: A repertoire to learn by name
paragraphs: The syllabus asks students to compare Odissi, Champu, Chhanda, Choutisha, Geeta Govinda and other devotional compositions. Its practical papers include selected Champu songs, Chhanda and Ashtapadi passages from Geeta Govinda. These are names to carry into a conversation with a singer, each attached to particular works and ways of learning.

For a newcomer, one song is enough to begin. Ask its title, the poet’s name and the name used for its musical form. Then ask who taught this rendition. A title identifies something you can return to; a teacher’s name begins a different story, about how the singing reached this person.

The curriculum is evidence of organised study in a particular academic period. It is not a listening lesson, an exhaustive map of every lineage or a notice that a course is currently accepting visitors.

blocks.title: Keep the musician in the picture
paragraphs: The Sangeet Natak Akademi’s register lists Sanjukta Panigrahi’s 1976 recognition as a joint award with Raghunath Panigrahi for Odissi music. The wording matters: the shared entry still names a distinct musical contribution.

That distinction is useful when reading a programme. A dancer may be the most visible person, yet a song arrives through other creative work. Keep the singer’s name alongside the dancer’s. When a programme supplies a composer or arranger, preserve that credit too. An award entry establishes recognition; it does not tell us which recording we are hearing or who wrote its words.

blocks.title: One poem, several creative roles
paragraphs: Bijayini Satpathy’s production page for ABHIPSAA — A Seeking (2021) makes those roles unusually clear. Virahī draws on Raghunath Panigrahi’s song composition of an Ashtapadi from Jayadeva’s Geet Govind. The page names Bindhumalini Narayanaswamy as singer, Srinibas Satapathy for prelude composition, melodic arrangement and flute, and Shivshankar Satapathy for rhythm composition, Mardala and manjira. Satpathy is credited with concept and choreography.

Here the poet, song composer, singer, arranger and rhythm musician are identifiable people. Their contributions meet in one production. Reading those credits helps us resist assigning everything we hear to the name most prominent on a poster.
This is an example from a documented work, not a claim that every Odissi ensemble uses the same instruments or arrangement. No recording of the production has been auditioned for this article.

blocks.title: Keeping songs available to learn
paragraphs: The Odissi Research Centre’s institutional handbook describes its establishment in July 1986 and work on both dance and music. Its publication account names cassette volumes of Kishore Chandrananda Champu, with lyrics by Kavisurya Baladev Rath, and a notation book with accompanying cassettes called Champu-Sarani. It also describes Chhanda notation work.

A written notation and a recorded rendition preserve different kinds of detail. Together they suggest a research path: locate the edition, identify its singers and teachers, and compare what the written and sounded versions can tell us. The handbook documents preservation activity; it does not confirm that those editions are now for sale or freely available online.

These institutional dates are not dates when the music began. Establishing an earlier history requires closer work with texts, editions and practitioners. For now, begin with one credited song, listen with patience, and leave space for the singer’s explanation.

limits: Desk-researched introduction. No independent practitioner or language review, field encounter or auditioned audio.
